what_its_for: This medicine is an inhaled corticosteroid (steroid) used to control and prevent asthma symptoms such as wheezing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. It works by reducing swelling and irritation in your airways to make breathing easier. It is NOT a rescue inhaler and will NOT stop an asthma attack that has already started.
how_to_take: 1. If using QVAR RediHaler, you do NOT need to shake it or prime it before use. Simply open the cap and inhale. 2. If using a traditional QVAR inhaler, shake it well before each use. 3. Breathe out fully to empty your lungs. 4. Place the mouthpiece in your mouth and close your lips around it. 5. Breathe in slowly and deeply through your mouth as you press down on the inhaler. 6. Hold your breath for about 10 seconds, then breathe out slowly. 7. If your doctor told you to take more than one puff, wait about 30 seconds between puffs. 8. VERY IMPORTANT: Rinse your mouth with water and spit it out after each use. Do NOT swallow the water. This helps prevent a mouth infection called thrush (a yeast infection in your mouth).
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you. The typical doses are: Adults and teenagers (12 years and older): 40 to 320 micrograms (mcg) inhaled twice daily. Children (5 to 11 years): 40 mcg inhaled twice daily. Always use this medicine exactly as your doctor prescribed. Do not use more or less than directed. Use it at the same times every day, even when you feel fine.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep the inhaler away from heat, open flames, and direct sunlight. Do NOT puncture or throw the canister into a fire or incinerator, even when it is empty. Keep out of reach of children. Do not store in the bathroom where it can get damp.
what_to_avoid: Do NOT use this inhaler as a rescue inhaler during a sudden asthma attack. Always have a separate fast-acting (rescue) inhaler, such as albuterol, available. Avoid smoking, as it can make your asthma worse and reduce how well this medicine works. Avoid known asthma triggers such as allergens, dust, or strong fumes. Do not stop using this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor, even if you feel better.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you notice: white patches or sores inside your mouth or on your tongue (signs of thrush or yeast infection); your breathing gets worse or you need your rescue inhaler more than usual; vision problems or eye pain; signs of low adrenal function such as unusual tiredness, weakness, nausea, vomiting, or dizziness; signs of allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or severe dizziness; a child using this medicine seems to be growing more slowly than expected. In case of a sudden asthma attack that does not improve with your rescue inhaler, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room immediately.
when_it_works: This medicine does NOT work right away. It may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use before you notice improvement in your asthma symptoms. Full benefit may take 4 to 6 weeks of daily use. Keep using it every day as prescribed, even if you feel fine. It only works when taken regularly.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using this medicine if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Poorly controlled asthma during pregnancy can be harmful, so your doctor will help weigh the risks and benefits. Children: This medicine is approved for children 5 years and older. Long-term use of inhaled steroids may slow growth in some children. Your doctor will monitor your child's height regularly. Older adults: No special dose adjustment is usually needed, but older adults should be watched for bone thinning (osteoporosis) with long-term use. Patients with active infections: Tell your doctor if you have a current viral, bacterial, or fungal infection. Inhaled steroids may make some infections harder to fight.
